newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle Atlantis heads for Russia's Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle Atlantis heads for Russia's Mir.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis rocketed off its Florida launch pad in a brilliant blast of light and smoke on Thursday, headed for Russia's Mir space station.
The $2 billion reusable spaceship carried a seven-member multi-national crew into a cloudless night sky at 4:07 a.m. EDT (0807 GMT) after a nearly flawless three-day countdown.
The on-time takeoff meant the shuttle was on schedule to dock with the Russian orbiting space outpost at 10:34 p.m. EDT on Friday night (0234 GMT Saturday).
Atlantis was to pick up Jerry Linenger, who has been working aboard Mir since January, and drop off his replacement, Michael Foale.

"We're on our way," shuttle commander Charles Precourt said in Russian moments after the shuttle leapt off its launch pad. His words echoed those used by Yuri Gagarin at his historic blastoff in 1961, NASA spokesman Rob Navias said.

Valentina Tereshkova, who in 1963 became the first woman in space, watched the predawn blastoff from a nearby viewing site. As Atlantis streaked skyward, she hugged Valeri Ryumin, a former cosmonaut and husband of Atlantis' Russian crew member Elena Kondakova.
NASA Administrator Daniel Goldin and Russian space officials toasted the successful blastoff with vodka.
Atlantis completed its fiery climb to orbit in less than nine minutes. The shuttle's bright engines were still visible to observers at the launch site when it was more than 480 miles (772 km) out.

The Mir space station was soaring high above the Indian Ocean west of Australia when the shuttle blasted off and its crew were unable to see the launch. Mir's Russian commander, Vasily Tsibliev, did however report seeing the shuttle's brightly lit launch pad through binoculars as the station later passed overhead.
"That's great," Linenger said after being informed of the successful launch.
The shuttle's crew, which includes a woman pilot, a Russian woman, a Frenchman, natives of Britain and Peru, and an astronaut of Chinese descent, is one of the most diverse selected by NASA.
Joining two-time shuttle flier Precourt on the shuttle's flight deck was Eileen Collins, who became NASA's first woman shuttle pilot in February 1995.
Also on board was Foale, the British-born astronaut Atlantis is ferrying to Mir, and Kondakova, a cosmonaut who spent 169-days aboard Mir in 1994 and 1995.
Rounding out the crew were mission specialists Jean-Francois Clervoy, a French astronaut from European Space Agency; Edward Lu, an astrophysicist; and Carlos Noriega, who was born in Lima, Peru.
The shuttle's blastoff began a two-day chase through space to catch up with Mir, where U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger is nearing the end of a four-month tour of duty.

The 42-year-old navy captain and medical doctor will be relieved by Foale, who is to live and work on Mir until mid-September. Foale, who is married with two young children, will be the fifth NASA astronaut to stay on the Russian station.
Foale was trained to help his cosmonaut crewmates maintain the 11-year-old space station, which has suffered numerous mechanical breakdowns, one of which led to a serious fire in February.
Atlantis is carrying 4,000 lbs (1,814 kg) of supplies and equipment to Mir, including a replacement oxygen generator and repair gear to patch up a leaky cooling system.
